title: Senior's toolkit: subnets in practice
summary: Check a CIDR plan with a calculator, add and inspect addresses, and test IPv6, instead of doing binary in your head under pressure.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: subnets in practice
steps.body: You learned the arithmetic so you can reason about it. At work you still check every plan with a tool before it goes into Terraform or a firewall rule, because one wrong prefix length is an outage.

toolkit.what: Prints the mask, network, broadcast, first and last host and the host count for a prefix. Quick proof that a range is what you think.
flags: Debian/Ubuntu `ipcalc` package only: split the block into subnets for those host counts
RHEL/Fedora `ipcalc` (Debian package `ipcalc-ng`): split into /26s; there `-s` means silent
the two programs share a name but not their flags; both print network, HostMin, HostMax and host count

toolkit.what: The `ipaddress` module ships with Python everywhere. Use it to split blocks, test membership and check overlaps in a script or a CI check.
flags: is this address inside that block?

toolkit.what: Adds an address with its prefix to an interface (until reboot). The prefix matters: it decides which hosts the machine thinks are local.
flags: always give the prefix; without it you get a /32
toolkit.example: sudo ip addr add 192.168.50.2/24 dev eth1

toolkit.what: The IPv6 addresses on each interface. Expect a `fe80::/64` link-local on every interface plus any global ones from SLAAC or DHCPv6.
flags: the IPv6 routing table and default gateway

toolkit.what: Tests IPv6 reachability on its own. When an app is slow only on some networks, broken IPv6 that clients try first is a classic cause.
flags: the same choice for an HTTP test

toolkit.what: Windows: every address with its prefix length per interface, as objects you can filter.
flags: the classic text view, including DHCP and DNS servers

steps.prompt: Match each prefix to how many addresses it holds.
A new VPC peering fails to route, and the cloud console says `overlapping CIDR`. One side is `10.0.0.0/16`. Which one-liner proves which of the other side's subnets collides?
options: `python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; print(i.ip_network('10.0.0.0/16').overlaps(i.ip_network('10.0.128.0/20')))"` for each of its subnets
steps.explain: Overlap is a property of the two ranges, not of any packet, so check it with a calculator. Put the same check in CI next to your Terraform and the mistake never reaches a peering request.

steps.prompt: You ran `sudo ip addr add 10.20.4.10 dev eth0` on a new VM. It can reach its gateway at `10.20.4.1` only after you add a route by hand. What went wrong?
options: No prefix was given, so the address is a /32 and no neighbour is on-link; it should be `10.20.4.10/22`
steps.explain: Without a prefix the kernel adds a /32, so it has no connected route for the rest of the subnet. With `/22` it adds `10.20.4.0/22 dev eth0` automatically.

steps.code: python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; [print(n) for n in i.ip_network('10.8.0.0/22').__1__(new_prefix=__2__)]"
steps.explain: `subnets(new_prefix=24)` yields 10.8.0.0/24 to 10.8.3.0/24, four in all. `supernet()` goes the other way, `hosts()` lists single addresses.

steps.prompt: What is the last usable host address that `ipcalc` reports for this block?
steps.explain: A /26 is 64 addresses: 192.168.10.64 to .127. .64 is the network, .127 the broadcast, so hosts run from .65 to .126.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Never type a CIDR into a firewall rule, Terraform or a cloud console without checking it in `ipcalc` or Python first. Keep the overlap check in CI for your network plan, and test `-4` and `-6` separately whenever a problem only shows up on some networks.
